# Proof

Notation: $\N = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$; for a function $f$ with values in $\R$ and a finite set $F$ of its domain, $s_f(F) := \sum_{i\in F} f(i)$ (with $s_f(\emptyset)=0$). "Countable" means finite or countably infinite, i.e. admitting an injection into $\N$. The generalized sum $\sum_{i\in J} f(i)$ converges to $L$ iff the net $F\mapsto s_f(F)$, indexed by finite subsets $F\subseteq J$ directed by inclusion, converges to $L$.

**Lemma A.** Let $f:J\to[0,\infty)$. The generalized sum $\sum_{i\in J} f(i)$ converges iff $\{s_f(F): F\subseteq J \text{ finite}\}$ is bounded above, and then its value is $\sup_F s_f(F)$.

*Proof.* Since $f\ge 0$, $F\subseteq G$ implies $s_f(F)\le s_f(G)$. If the set is bounded above, let $L$ be its supremum. Given $\varepsilon>0$ pick finite $F_0$ with $s_f(F_0)>L-\varepsilon$; for every finite $F\supseteq F_0$, $L-\varepsilon<s_f(F_0)\le s_f(F)\le L$. So the net converges to $L$; limits of nets in $\R$ are unique, so the value is $L$. Conversely, if the net converges to $L'$, pick finite $F_0$ with $|s_f(F)-L'|<1$ for all finite $F\supseteq F_0$; then for any finite $G$, $s_f(G)\le s_f(G\cup F_0)<L'+1$, so the set is bounded. $\square$

**Lemma B.** Let $g:\N\to[0,\infty)$. The series $\sum_{n=0}^\infty g(n)$ converges iff $\{s_g(G): G\subseteq\N\text{ finite}\}$ is bounded above, and then $\sum_{n=0}^\infty g(n)=\sup_G s_g(G)$.

*Proof.* The partial sums $p_N=s_g(\{0,\dots,N\})$ never decrease, so the series converges iff $(p_N)$ is bounded above, and then its sum is $\sup_N p_N$ (monotone convergence). Every $p_N$ is some $s_g(G)$, and every finite $G$ lies in some $\{0,\dots,N\}$ with $s_g(G)\le p_N$ since $g\ge0$. Hence the two sets have the same upper bounds, so the same boundedness and the same supremum. $\square$

**Lemma C.** Let $f:J\to[0,\infty)$, $T\subseteq J$ with $f(i)=0$ for $i\notin T$. Then $\{s_f(F):F\subseteq J\text{ finite}\}=\{s_f(F):F\subseteq T\text{ finite}\}$.

*Proof.* $s_f(F)=s_f(F\cap T)$ and $F\cap T$ is a finite subset of $T$; the other inclusion is trivial. $\square$

**Lemma D.** Let $S$ be a set, $\varphi:S\to\N$ injective, $f:S\to[0,\infty)$, and $g:\N\to[0,\infty)$ with $g(\varphi(i))=f(i)$ for $i\in S$ and $g(n)=0$ for $n\notin\varphi(S)$. Then $\{s_g(G):G\subseteq\N\text{ finite}\}=\{s_f(F):F\subseteq S\text{ finite}\}$.

*Proof.* For finite $G\subseteq\N$, let $F=\varphi^{-1}(G)$, finite since $\varphi$ is injective; $\varphi$ restricts to a bijection $F\to G\cap\varphi(S)$, so $s_g(G)=s_g(G\cap\varphi(S))=\sum_{i\in F}g(\varphi(i))=s_f(F)$. For finite $F\subseteq S$, $G=\varphi(F)$ is finite and likewise $s_g(G)=s_f(F)$. $\square$

## Construction

Let $x_1,\dots,x_m\in A$ (if $m=0$ there is nothing to prove). For each $a$, $S_a=\{i\in I: x_a(i)\ne0\}$ is countable by (1); choose injections $\psi_a:S_a\to\N$. Let $S=S_1\cup\dots\cup S_m$. The map $i\mapsto(\min\{a: i\in S_a\},\psi_{\min\{a:i\in S_a\}}(i))$ is an injection $S\to\N\times\N$ (if two points have the same image they lie in the same $S_a$ and have equal $\psi_a$-value). Composing with the injection $\N\times\N\to\N$, $(p,q)\mapsto 2^p3^q$, gives an injection $\varphi:S\to\N$.

Define, for $a=1,\dots,m$ and $n\in\N$:
$$y_a(n)=\begin{cases}x_a(i)&\text{if } n=\varphi(i),\ i\in S,\\ 0&\text{if } n\notin\varphi(S).\end{cases}$$
This is well defined as $\varphi$ is injective. Note $x_a(i)=0$ for $i\notin S$.

**Key identity.** For any $a,b$ (possibly equal, and allowing the zero function in place of $x_b$, with $y_b$ then the zero sequence), put $f_{ab}(i)=(x_a(i)-x_b(i))^2$ on $I$ and $g_{ab}(n)=(y_a(n)-y_b(n))^2$ on $\N$. Then $f_{ab}\ge0$ vanishes off $S$, and $g_{ab}(\varphi(i))=f_{ab}(i)$ for $i\in S$, $g_{ab}(n)=0$ for $n\notin\varphi(S)$. By Lemmas C and D,
$$\{s_{g_{ab}}(G):G\subseteq\N\text{ finite}\}=\{s_{f_{ab}}(F):F\subseteq S\text{ finite}\}=\{s_{f_{ab}}(F):F\subseteq I\text{ finite}\}.\tag{$*$}$$

**$y_a\in\ell^2$.** Take $x_b=0$: $f(i)=x_a(i)^2$, $g(n)=y_a(n)^2$. By (2) and Lemma A the right side of $(*)$ is bounded above, hence so is the left, and by Lemma B $\sum_n y_a(n)^2$ converges. So $y_1,\dots,y_m\in\ell^2$.

**Distances.** For finite $F\subseteq I$, $(x_a(i)-x_b(i))^2\le 2x_a(i)^2+2x_b(i)^2$ gives $s_{f_{ab}}(F)\le 2\sum_{i\in I}x_a(i)^2+2\sum_{i\in I}x_b(i)^2$ (using Lemma A's supremum bound). Thus by Lemma A, $\sum_{i\in I}(x_a(i)-x_b(i))^2$ converges and equals $\sup$ of the right side of $(*)$. By $(*)$ and Lemma B, $\sum_{n\ge0}(y_a(n)-y_b(n))^2$ converges to the same supremum. Taking nonnegative square roots, $d_{\ell^2}(y_a,y_b)=d_2(x_a,x_b)$ for all $a,b\in[1,m]$.

**Equality pattern.** If $x_a=x_b$ then $y_a=y_b$ directly from the definition. If $y_a=y_b$, then for $i\in S$, $x_a(i)=y_a(\varphi(i))=y_b(\varphi(i))=x_b(i)$, and for $i\notin S$, $x_a(i)=0=x_b(i)$; so $x_a=x_b$. Hence $y_a\ne y_b\iff x_a\ne x_b$.

This proves the claim. $\blacksquare$
